utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we have in the witness, there's just one matter I would like to seek to a response from the Prosecution. Last Friday we received a new expert report, and today the Defence filed their objections for the tendering of this report. I wonder whether the Prosecution would like to make a reply at this stage. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I would. The difficulty is that I sort of got this almost as I was coming into court and I haven't really had time to digest it. It won't take that long. Would it be -- could I do that at the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. You know, of course you are entitled to have some time to digest it and to make your positions at a later stage, but I have to remind the parties that we have to make a ruling as early as possible. Yes, could we have the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, there are in fact a number of matters that I have to raise before we move to the witness. Your Honours, there -- the first one is one which we were going to deal with at the start of today's proceedings, but Ms. Chana, I'm told, is unable to be here, and that is the matter of the outstanding exhibits that had been offered for tender. Now, she's not here and I'm just simply not sure what the position is about Ms. Chana. So I don't know that my learned friend is in a position to respond from what he's mentioned to me. Perhaps the Prosecutors can tell you what the position is about that in a moment. In any event, the Prosecutors not being in a position to respond to that, I don't think -- well, I don't know what Your Honour wishes to have done about that. Because we had in mind to finish that, Mr. Delalic having finished his evidence last week, we didn't do that. There was on the Defence side three outstanding letters and on the Prosecution side, there was two documents. I don't think we can do those now, Your Honour, because Ms. Chana is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether you have changed your positions concerning of the two documents tendered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, it really was pending a further discussion with my learned friend, unfortunately, and she's not here. At this stage, yes, no, we still do, we reserve our position about this. There's something that I have to clarify with her, and it really depends -- not that it's negotiating, Your Honour, but we have to have another discussion before we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could deal with it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases. Okay, Your Honours, the next matter that has to arise is another one concerning Mr. Ramiz Delalic, Celo. There was, as you'll recall, a request in for extra material concerning Mr. Delalic. And as the cross-examination unfolded you will remember hat it became clear that he had given statements which we don't have to two different sets of Prosecution investigators; those in 1996 and of course Mr. Mikhailov in 1998. We don't have those statements. In addition, there was a third lot of statements which we don't have and that is those which are referred to in the indictment, which we tendered. Your Honours will remember there was an indictment raised and in fact a judgement entered -- I don't think we even tendered the indictment, I'm sorry, I apologise for that. We tendered the judgement. It was the one where it all proceeded in front of Judge Hadzic and there was a little bit of trouble in the court on that occasion, Your Honours, and on that occasion, in the judgement at least two other statements are referred to in the course of the judgement because there was an occasion where Mr. Delalic came into the court, the things happened which were the subject of the indictment, and then he signed. And that was in April. That's not the document that we've got. So that's -- would appear to be three different occasions when Mr. Delalic has said something to investigators of various sorts, and we don't have any of those. So the Defence has requested from the Prosecutor those statements and an account, if they haven't got them, of what happened to them. And I was rather hoping today that we might get a response from the Prosecutors there, but Ms. Chana is not here so we might not. But I think perhaps we'd better clarify with the Prosecutors what the position is about that, if that's possible, before I say anymore about it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, are you in a position to answer the questions put to you by Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not. We just have a difficulty today and perhaps -- I don't know for how long throughout the week. Ms. Chana isn't here -- could we just go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, the expert matter we'll leave, as Your Honour's indicated. Now, there's one more matter of general concern that I have to raise, and that is concerning one document that the Prosecutor proposes to tender here. It's document 65 ter number 150. And it's a document that makes an allegation -- it's one of those operative information sort of documents and it's going to be put to this witness in some form or other. Now, Your Honours, we were very concerned with what happened to Mr. Delalic, that unanswerable allegations were made, that if we were to try to answer them all, we would be here until this time next here because Mr. Halilovic has plotted to kill the president -- sorry, to kill the commander-in-chief of the army, and there's numerous of those sort of things and many of them we didn't deal with on a step-by-step basis. Now we're about to get a new one, a new piece of information, and it just places the Defence in a position, Your Honours, where we can't control the allegations that are coming out now, they're flying thick and fast in a way -- we'll address you about them, of course, very strongly at the end, but we need to have some sense about what we have to answer and what we don't have to answer, because in looking at the Defence case now, we are considering whether we need to answer an allegation that Sefer Halilovic planned to kill Rasim Delic, which has never been said until we got here before. Now we have this document D150 which concerns Ramiz Delalic, an alleged joint criminal enterprise between Delalic and Sefer Halilovic, which is contained in there. Now, it's another one of these allegations which, Your Honour, it really places us in a difficult position to know how to answer it because it's got no direct connection at all to what happened here. As you'll see, it was not put at all to Mr. Delalic, who's just been here. But now in his absence something else is going to be put. Now, it really is for the Prosecutor to put the document as they see fit; it's up to them to run their own case, but it's a matter of to the Defence, and in my respectful submission it's a concern to the Tribunal as well, because if you have this spreading web of allegations, there could be all sorts of reasons for it. You might be dealing with the devil, Your Honours, but you might not be. But it places the Defence in the position of having to answer a multiplicity of allegations not pleaded in the indictment, way outside the indictment, poisonous and prejudicial if not answered, time-wasting and irrelevant if they are answered. If we prove that Sefer Halilovic didn't plan to kill Rasim Delic, we're no closer to an acquittal. It's just an irrelevant thing out there, but it's prejudicial. When that document comes, 150, it's a matter for the Prosecutors whether they seek to lead it or not, but I just raise this, that we will object to it, and I want them to know that because it's only recently we got the proofing notes, and obviously we're preparing this as we go. That document is going to be objected to, and when it is, Your Honour, that's going to be the chief thrust of it, that this material is just too remote, too far gone and too difficult to answer at short notice and outside of the indictment, and all of those matters. So I don't ask you to rule on it now and I hope the Prosecutors will reconsider using it, but if it comes, then that's the nature of the objection that's coming. The final matter is that we could ask for some indulgence of the court in terms of the timing of cross-examination here with this witness. In respect of this witness, there is a great deal of documentary background that may - and I stress the word "may" - become relevant depending upon what he says in court here. Now, we have been -- our resources have just been stretched too thinly to prepare that properly and I feel at the moment not sufficiently on top of the documents that I have to be ready to proceed. I want to take some instructions from Mr. Halilovic on certain aspects. The fact is we can't see him on weekends; it's not a facility that's available to us. So, Your Honours, what I ask is that depending on the progress of cross-examination -- sorry, evidence in chief here, that we not be called upon to cross-examine him today. I could deal with some aspects of it. If it appears that I would be comfortable to deal with those, I will advise the Court and say I'm happy to start, but I frankly do concede a sense of being unprepared. There's a variety of reasons, and preparedness actually saves time. So can I just foreshadow that I'm likely to ask that when the cross-examination time comes, we're going to ask that it be -- that we have an indulgence of some period of time and I'll see how it unfolds before I put a figure on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Those are the matters I wish to raise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe the last request is reasonable, but however we will make our ruling depends on the progress of the direct examination and how it goes. And please remind us if you really feel it's necessary to have a short break for you to prepare your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, I would be grateful for that, and we'll see how the evidence unfolds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So I believe it's high time for us to have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I can't hear you. I'm sorry. Would you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Bakir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is your date of birth the 1st of October, 1956?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 1st of October, 1956, born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And are you a businessman?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have a -- are you an authorised Volkswagen dealer in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have a coffee roasting business?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It's a business relating to espresso machines, but in essence, yes, that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you involved in any other business activities at the moment?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: No, that's all that I'm involved in currently.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you do your JNA service in 1977 and 1978?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What diploma do you hold?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I have a BA in political sciences and I majored in defence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, faculty for political sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And from 1978 until 1984, did you work as a security officer for Energoinvest?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that that's true, although the formulation could be somewhat amended. I was an officer -- security officer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From 1984 until 1992, did you work in state security in Bosnia, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In -- just generally, which area did you work in?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I worked at the service. The scope of my work at the time was what was then known as the issues related to the Ustasha immigration.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in spring of 1992, were you appointed to the position of the chief of police in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: That's right, although the full formulation was chief of the security services centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did that mean, the full formulation, that you were the police chief of the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities and duties, as briefly as you can possibly tell us.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The security services are -- deal with public security, meaning everything relating to the security of the citizens. That also involved criminal investigations, and they have criminal investigation policemen working for them. So everything that covers public security; security of facilities, citizens, and everything else that the term encompasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that within the responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The security services centre is an organisational unit of the Ministry of the Interior, and the minister was my superior. Not just mine but also he was a superior of all other chiefs of other services. Sarajevo centre was just one of the centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many police did you have working for you when you were the police chief in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: At the time, there were somewhere up to 1500 policemen. Later on, that number increased sharply, in view of the developments in Bosnia at the time, meaning that the reserve police forces were augmented in terms of the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In June 1993, were you appointed as the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you hold that position until 1995, when you were appointed as the director of AID, which was the Bosnian State Security?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I remained minister of the interior until the end of 1995 and was then appointed director of AID.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you remain in that position until March 1996, when you were made an assistant to the minister for foreign affairs, a position you held until 1997?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Perhaps it was 1997 to 1998 that I worked at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as assistant minister for consular and visa affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were your duties as the minister of interior from June 1993 onwards? What were your areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: At the time, at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, there were two segments, two fields; dealing with public security and state security. Within the field of public security, as I've already told you, there were the security services centres, whereas within the state security field there was the chief of the service who had -- who was quite powerful within that level.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, can you just repeat the last part of your answer. The interpreters didn't quite catch it.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: As I've said, the chief of the secret service was an official who was quite autonomous, had a large autonomy within his work in commanding the work of secret services. He had to consult with the minister only on certain issues that are regulated by the rules of the secret service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you responsible to the -- or report to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the minister for the interior?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, in view of the fact that the war had already started, I was directly responsible to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in accordance with the then-regulations, there was a system of armed forces, including the Ministry of the Interior, and all of them were subordinated to the Presidency, which had command authority over these services. Although all other issues relating to status, logistics, and so on were dealt with by the government, by the state government. And I as a minister was also a member of the cabinet, a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you also a member of an enlarged Presidency during that time in the war?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: That was an unwritten rule. This issue was not regulated by any actual provisions. It is just that as a result of the war, ministers had to inform the Presidency, brief the members of the Presidency on certain issues, and so on, although, at the time, there were no regulations providing that this is how it ought to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you attend meetings of the Presidency at all?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Upon invitation. When asked by the Presidency to attend, I would attend meetings. Not every single meeting, I would not attend them regularly, but would come only upon invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did the Presidency require your presence at some meetings?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the reason for that was that certain issues were discussed, the issues that fall within the scope of authorities of police or Ministry of the Interior. For example, when they needed to be briefed on the security situation, on the situation on the ground, on the human rights violations, or other issues that fall within the jurisdiction of the Presidency and that the Presidency needed to decide upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, during the war were police used in combat in coordination with the military?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: During the war, police was always an active participant in the defence of the country, and it was used, police forces were used, together with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in concert with them. And in that context, the police organised itself in parallel as these events were unfolding. Special units were established within the Ministry of the Interior which were most often used in combat operations. And in those combat operations, these police units would always be resubordinated to the army, meaning that the army was always in command. They would plan, organise, and command all combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the process of transferring subordination of the special police units to the command of the army?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It was simple: There would be a document to indicate that a unit was resubordinated to the army. The unit commander would receive some sort of document that would indicate who he should report to about that, so that was that. Obviously there would be a previous agreement and a request that had been made by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your signature required to subordinate -- I'm sorry, to transfer the police units to army command or could you delegate that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In principle, the assistant minister for police would have been in charge of the police. He could have issued an order, having previously consulted with me and other bodies within the army, to send a unit to carry out a certain mission or to go to an area. The assistant minister for police would have been authorised to do that, but the minister would always be informed that a certain unit was being sent to carry out a mission, especially if this was a MUP unit. The Interior Ministry had a special police squad called Bosna. They were often involved in combat operations. When something like this occurred, the minister would have been told the kind of missions and tasks that the unit was carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the strength of this Bosna unit?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It grew in the war. At first it had several hundred members, and towards the end of the war it had nearly a thousand men, including the reserve forces. So this is a ballpark figure for both active and reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about a unit called Laste? For the transcript, that's L-a-s-t-e. What was that unit?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: That was another special unit of the security services centre Sarajevo. All the others, the security service centres, had the same kind of unit; Tuzla, Zenica, Mostar, the whole lot of them. And this was something that was organised by the Interior Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the strength of the Laste Unit?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: This also changed over time. I think when it was first established it had about 50 members. Gradually it grew to comprise about as many as 100 or possibly 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was its function in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: First and foremost its function in Sarajevo was in its capacity as a special unit. When it was first used, it would be used by the police and used to protect citizens and property; to protect law and order, to protect citizens and property. And if necessary, it could also be used for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When and how was it formed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: By coincidence, I had only just arrived from Sarajevo. I think it was formed on the 15th of May, 1992, in Sarajevo. Having previously obtained authorisation from the minister of the interior, I signed the decision on the establishment of this unit. So that's how the unit came into existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of equipment did this unit have?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In peacetime, before this unit was established, we had another unit that was very much like this unit. It had the same sort of equipment that this new unit would later have. As for this new unit, it had whatever it could be given at the time. And the equipment it was given was a bit newer and a bit better, and this was on account of the sort of tasks that it was facing. It had to deal with certain individuals and certain groups, and it was very often deployed along the front line to keep the enemy forces from getting closer to Sarajevo. It had a bit more equipment and a bit more weapons than the regular police forces, which went about a very different set of tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of weaponry did it have in comparison to the regular police forces?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: They had long barrels, rifles, automatic weapons, whereas the police units for the most part had pistols and whatever was at hand. And this was sufficient for them to go about their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How often was the Laste Unit used in combat by the military?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that this unit comprised highly trained people, dedicated people, brave people, brave fighters, well, you have to know that these men were trained as the unit was being built, but the human resources were very good and this was soon recognised, the fact that this unit was able to hold certain lines to keep the enemy from breaking into Sarajevo, so that whenever necessary this unit was used. Quite often, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it used outside of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The unit was used outside Sarajevo whenever the need arose, and it gave a great contribution. I think if you look at the statistics, I can't give you the statistics off the top of my head now, but I think this unit had a lot of numbers -- a lot of members who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did the military use this particular unit, the Laste Unit, when they were used in combat?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In principle, which was perfectly all right, the military would ask for help in order to perform combat operations. I don't wish to speak about the Laste unit separately, because there are other units that should be considered. For example, the MUP special unit. I don't think the Laste unit merits being singled out for special treatment because all the units had the same treatment and all the units were used in combat operations. So that, for example, whenever the 1st Corps or another unit of the military required the assistance of this unit for combat operations, whenever the unit was available, whenever its members were sufficiently rested, whenever it had sufficient equipment and weapons, there was no need not to resubordinate this unit for whatever purposes its assistance was requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did your job as minister of the interior involve travel outside of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It was my job and my duty and also my personal desire to be involved in all the organisational units of the Ministry of the Interior on account of the wartime circumstances. And to the extent that I could, I would travel further afield, meet the heads of the various centres and help them resolve any problems that they had. Therefore, I can say that I travelled all over Bosnia, far and wide throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever travel with the special units when they went to combat with the military?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The -- let me put it this way: I never travelled with them using the same vehicle or exactly at the same time as they were travelling, but I often went to see where these units would be deployed and where they would be fighting in order to help them, especially with people I knew, the police chiefs, to help them in terms of logistics, in terms of supplies, in terms of accommodations, so that the units would face as little hardship on the ground as possible. I travelled between Bihac, Central Bosnia, and all the way to Mostar with these units. I covered a lot of ground with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever meet the army commanders to whom these units were to be subordinated in combat?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think we all kept meeting all the time. It wasn't an area large enough to allow you not to meet certain people. It was a relatively small area, a relatively small area with lots of combat operations going on. So those of us who moved about that area would often meet, talk, exchange our opinions and experiences in order to find better solutions and get better results and in order to find solutions that would be best for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know the accused, Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long have you known him for?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think we met just before the war. Roughly speaking, that was the time we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In general terms - and I'll move to the specifics a little later - what was the relationship like between army units stationed in Sarajevo in 1993 and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can say anything good about the relationship. You're asking me to assess what the relationship was like. There was a lot of tension, especially out in the field. The units were armed, there were all kinds of persons in these units, all with their own traits and natures. Some of them were aggressive. There were a lot of problems which made the relationship between the police and the BH army quite complex at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the cause of the tension -- I'm sorry. A moment ago you said the units were armed. Were you referring to the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Both. Both were armed to the extent possible, respectively. Both the army and the police were poorly armed to begin with. They had what they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the cause of the tension between the army and the police in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Incidents were frequent. Certain members -- if you look at it from my point of view as someone who was the chief of the Security Services Centre at the time, certain members of the army wanted to loot certain areas of town, certain shops, to raid certain flats. There was a lot being done by individuals at the time who were trying to take over some of the police tasks which they believed they should have been doing. This was something that the police, as an institution, could no longer tolerate. So there were certain differences which resulted in incidents and clashes. Sometimes these were major incidents, sometimes not so major. This is something that was dealt with by the command bodies, but the fact remains that these clashes and incidents did occur. I think a lot was done about that by the former minister, Jusuf Pusina, and General Sefer Halilovic to resolve these matters, but the situation was very complex and things kept on happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From which units were the members of the army that were involved in attempting to loot certain areas of town, certain shops, raiding certain flats, and so on?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, there were many such individuals, but such incidents were particularly frequent in the case of this unit. It's been a long time, so I may not get the unit right, but I think it was Ramiz Delalic's unit, it was Caco's unit, it was the unit led by Jusuf Prazina. For the most part these were the units causing most of the incidents and trouble around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was Jusuf Prazina's unit known as?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: One must have a lot of respect for the military contribution of his unit also. Just because there were certain misfits in his unit, no one can deny their military contribution and the protection they afforded the town to a certain extent. But some members of that unit acted as some sort of a paramilitary unit, which did whatever it pleased. Prazina himself had no respect for anyone in high positions; the president, General Halilovic, or myself, for that matter. He had no respect for anyone. He was a renegade and a renegade from reason, if I may put it that way, and this is precisely the way he acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you become aware of the activities of members of Caco and Celo's -- sorry, Ramiz Delalic and Caco's units?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In the end, it was all very simple. When incidents occurred related to the ID'ing of the perpetrators, information was obtained based on their statements that they belonged to such-and-such units. The citizens themselves, after all, very often would come and report certain matters, usually very bad things done by these people. They would take people trench-digging of their own accord, they would mobilise people of their own accord, they would search flats of their own accord, without any proper authorisation, and they were involved in criminal activities also. This was regularly indicated by various police reports which, as a rule, reached me. This was something that was generally known in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of the Interior communicate with the military about these criminal reports the MUP was receiving?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: We did communicate, yes. A procedural decision was taken to do this through certain bodies. The security service centres -- or rather, the Ministry of the Interior would send written reports to the army command, to the Presidency, and to other relevant bodies. There was a need to familiarise these bodies so that they could get involved in solving these matters. There was communication and information was definitely passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any meetings between MUP representatives and representatives of the military about these criminal activities?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: We had a number of meetings. The situation was really quite cumbersome on a account of a number of internal problems, plus we were facing a massive enemy offensive which jeopardised the existence of Sarajevo and its citizens. You must bear in mind the fact that Sarajevo was shelled on a daily basis, which means you have problems. So meetings were held in a bid to find solutions, but the whole thing took a long time and I think eventually proved very damaging for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said, "We had a number of meetings." Did you ever attend any meetings with the military about these matters?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: At the time when I was chief of the security services centre, I may have met a few times with the minister of the interior and General Halilovic. We reviewed this situation, this cumbersome situation, and we looked at solutions, but we didn't have a clue at the time, precisely on account of the fact that there was intense fighting activity going on and we were facing a problem to which we knew no solution. In my capacity as chief and based on the information I received, that would be about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The meetings with General Halilovic, were they when he was chief of the Main Staff; that is, the number one person in the army?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was chief of the security services centre, and he, the general, was the number one man in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you make any suggestions as to what could be done to resolve the problems of criminal activities by members of the military in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we talked a great deal and reviewed a number of options. Any option would have entailed a great deal of risk once we decided to tackle the problem. There was immediately the danger that the enemy units would seize Sarajevo while we were trying to resolve our own internal conflict, be it crime or scandalous behaviour by certain members of the army. So the situation we faced is that in dealing with these internal problems, we faced the risk of losing the town. The environment being what it was at the time, it was very difficult to take any decisions. I think once in particular we considered this, but no one came up with a specific proposal on what to do. There was an idea floated that people should be arrested on the way out of Sarajevo, so that would be a situation where it was easier to arrest them. It would have been easier to arrest them outside Sarajevo than inside Sarajevo; that was the idea. But still, you didn't know what would happen in Sarajevo in that case. So these were the sort of ideas that were floated and the ideas and proposals that people had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just on that, you said, "There was an idea floated that people should be arrested on the way out of Sarajevo." Which people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: That -- that included the key people; Caco, Celo, and some others, and their people from the units; "their."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that was an idea or a proposal that was floated at the time. Was that floated in a meeting between you and Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that we started that issue together. At the time, I believed that that was a problem that he saw, the problem of the situation in town. There was a problem and we needed to resolve it. We proposed to General Halilovic certain options in order to resolve that problem, and as to particular roles and who exactly needed to do what exactly, that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the options you proposed to General Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: We as police tended to believe that the criminal activity of these people needed to be terminated and that this negative criminal trend needed to be dealt with firmly because it presented just as great a danger to Sarajevo as the enemy activity. We had numerous complaints from the citizens of Sarajevo who wanted to leave the town precisely because of the situation. Some people at the time disappeared. We as police could not simply tolerate that. So we made proposals, we as civilian police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were these proposals or options that you proposed to General Halilovic? That's all I want you to tell us at the moment, if you could.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that it was then that we gave a proposal to use an occasion when these people would leave Sarajevo and arrest them then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was General Halilovic's response to that particular proposal?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I can't recall now what exactly the general said at the time. But at the time, we presented this as a problem and as a proposal, and General Halilovic did not have to state his opinion to us. This was the army problem, not a police problem. So we did not receive a specific answer from him; however, I took it that he understood the situation, that he wanted to resolve the problem himself. I know that this problem was raised at the highest level, the Presidency level, that the Presidency discussed this problem at various meetings based on the information supplied to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you ever present at meetings of the Presidency when that was -- this particular problem was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were members of the military present at any meetings of the Presidency when this particular problem was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that they attended some meetings. We as police also held some meetings, asking that the problem be resolved. This was done independent from the army because we were part of the civilian authorities, and as such, we had a duty and a right to ask that the problem be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to say now in relation to Operation Trebevic, which was in late October 1993, when these meetings -- sorry, when these problems were discussed at meetings of the Presidency which you attended?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was already minister of the interior, and in that capacity I attended these meetings where the plans, the proposals were reviewed in order to solve the problem. I think that the entire Presidency, and not just President Izetbegovic, participated in this problem in analysing it and deciding on it. There was a vast amount of information requiring that we do something about it. There were many incidents, murders, which were unresolved. And I think that the Presidency understood the entire situation, and that in the end we offered a plan to the Presidency. Later on, the plan was expanded. We had a coded name for the plan. The plan was known as the Trebevic plan and it offered a way to deal with the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A few moments ago in one of your previous answers you said: "Some people at the time disappeared. We as police could simply not tolerate that." What did you mean? What were you referring to when you said "people disappeared"?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Specifically, we had a complaint from some people. A woman, somebody's wife, would come in and say, "My husband was taken away. The soldiers came, took him away and my husband did not return. I know nothing further." So we received these types of information. And we had similar cases, registered cases, and it was our duty to search for these people. Sarajevo was under siege at the time, and it was very difficult to conduct an investigation under those circumstances. We didn't even have complete records, for example. People were leaving Sarajevo en masse at the time. Some people applied to join the units, and we don't know how reliable the records of the units were, whether they were complete and so on. And all of this made our job more difficult. So we simply registered what the problem -- what the source of all the problems was, and it seemed that the commands of these two units were the source of the problem. And it seemed that the solution, the best solution, would be to appoint new people to the command of these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The commands of which units -- are you still referring to Caco and Celo at the moment?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how often were you receiving reports that soldiers had taken civilians away and had not returned?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: We in the ministry, or rather in the CSB, in the security services centre, have records where all of this is registered. So all of the complaints are recorded. I don't think that the number of these persons is as high as the number of persons who were mistreated and so on, or as the number of robberies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the records -- I'll withdraw that. What reports did you receive of mistreatment, just in general terms?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Frequently that would entail physical mistreatment, beatings, arrest, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in that answer are you referring to members of Caco and Celo's units or other units?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: This applies mostly to these units, although at the time we also had a unit of Juka Prazina and some other units in one part of the town. However, the focus of our attention and efforts was directed at these two units because they created much greater problems than some smaller units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also, a few moments ago in one of your answers, referred to murders. Can you explain -- can you elaborate on that, please. You said, "There were unresolved murders."

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you any details regarding this, but what I had in mind were the murders that we investigated in Sarajevo in the course of the operation called Kazan. Most of the unsolved problems fell under that category and we tried to resolve it in conjunction with the army and the organs of the judicial system.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was Operation Kazan?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that, using the operative police terms, it started before the Trebevic operation and was completed -- was completed with the aid of information obtained through the Trebevic operation. What I received, the information that I received, helped resolve a lot of other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was -- which group was the target of Operation Kazan?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you could repeat the question. I'm not sure I understood it properly. I don't know what you mean by the word "group"; whether that means citizens or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: But all right. In relation to that, I can give you my point of view. I think that through the problem that we called Kazani, we learned that there were some corpses of the people of all ethnic backgrounds, although the dominant group was of Serbian ethnicity. There were also Bosniaks and Croats who were mistreated by a group of people, and the group of people was linked to the Caco's brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was this particular problem, called Kazani, ever discussed in meetings with the military that you attended?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Regarding Kazani --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: -- or the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Kazani.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that the Trebevic plan planned also for that activity which was planned together with the army and entailed the participation of both the police and the army. The army was to play the main role because this involved or was aimed against the army members. They needed to provide certain resources, whereas the equipment and the expertise was provided by the Ministry of the Interior, and the case has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Your Honours, I have an objection to this line of questioning now, and in fact it's an objection I made about a month ago as well in relation to this. Your Honours, the evidence as it's now fallen in this case makes it perfectly plain that there's no evidence at all of 10th Brigade participation. Now, we have no more crime scene witnesses to come, as I understand the position. Therefore, leading the evidence about Kazani -- I didn't interrupt this witness now because he was giving an account and he's entitled to give the account that he gave uninterrupted, I think, but the evidence now is absolutely lacking that the 10th Brigade had anything to do with the crime at Grabovica, and of course no one suggests that they were involved at Uzdol either. So now I object on the grounds of relevance to leading evidence about the 10th Brigade and whatever activities they might have been suspected of or indeed might have been proved at a later time to have been involved in. Because in the past my objection was met by a statement, which was quite a correct statement, frankly, that we haven't got to the end of the evidence yet as far as the crime scene goes, but I think we have now, Your Honours, and the 10th Brigade just haven't been proved to have been involved in the killings at Grabovica. Therefore, I object to any further evidence being led on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe the 10th Brigade was not involved in the killings in Grabovica, but if my memory is long enough I remember that someone from the 10th Brigade was involved in the burning of the bodies in Grabovica, which could be regarded a part of the murder actions. To be on the safe side, we'll allow the Prosecution to proceed with the issues concerning of the 10th Brigade, and later on, after the Prosecution finished the presentation of its case, we'll consider your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We understand that your objections always stands there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, as Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May I add, it also goes to the accused's mens rea. It's always been our case that the use of those troops, if known to have criminal propensities, both the 9th and the 10th, goes to his mens rea in using those troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm not going to debate on this issue at this stage. Let's continue with the testimony of this witness and maybe we could take a break at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to move to another incident, Mr. Alispahic, and that is involving Senad Pecar. Now, what happened to --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Pecar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, what happened to Senad Pecar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In view of the time that has passed, I can't tell you specifically, but it was sometime during the summer, July or August, when a need arose to interview Senad Pecar about the criminal activity of himself and his associates. As a result of that, he was taken into custody and was -- by the military police, if I remember correctly. I couldn't tell you exactly where he was taken, but the reaction to his arrest was such that the 9th Mountain Brigade blocked the entire town, paying special attention to the old part of the town where those units converged. It was difficult for the citizens to move about the town. Certain facilities were blocked by the members of that unit who were armed. And the situation was such that we needed to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was Senad Pecar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Senad Pecar was assistant or deputy, I'm not sure which, but he was within the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which facilities were blocked by members of the 9th?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In addition to main thoroughfares, I think that the operative staff of the Supreme Command was blocked, the army hall was blocked as well, and that was it. They demanded to speak to somebody in order to resolve what they saw as problems. Their demand was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise for speaking over the interpreter. Who was "they"?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Members of these brigades and their leadership; Caco, Celo. They were -- there were also members of the Delta Unit as well. So there was a certain number of members of these units who believed that they had the identical problem or a similar problem, and they demanded that they meet with somebody in order to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How was the situation resolved?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It was resolved in such a way that we had to enter the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And who's "we"?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think the army hall, because the name of the building kept changing. So I think at the time it was called the army hall. General Delic and I were supposed to come to the meeting in order to respond to the demands that they placed before us. The commands of these two units said that they had certain problems, they wanted the problems to be resolved, and that it was the commander of the army and perhaps the head of the MUP who were supposed to resolve the problem in case where certain issues fell under the Ministry of the Interior, the issues relating to mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying there was a meeting in an army hall between you and General Delic, Caco, and Celo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: There were some other senior officers from those units there as well. I can't remember them right now. There were a lot of troops there. The entire army hall was blocked by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the Delta Unit, were the commanders of the Delta Unit there as well?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that one of the commanders of the Delta Unit was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did, to your knowledge, Mr. Halilovic have anything to do with this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that he was involved in any way. I don't think that he was. I don't think that General Halilovic was present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You referred to facilities being blocked. What about the police station in Centar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The police station in Centar - I can't remember the name of the street - was also blocked by these members. This was a result of the antagonism that prevailed between the police on the one hand and the army on the other at the time. The police station was held for a couple of hours, was kept under blockade, then the commander came. They disarmed a number of police officers, about a dozen of them were taken away to dig trenches. Some were physically mistreated and abused and we had to bring in stronger police forces to re-take the station, the police structure, and to bring it back under the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's take a break. We'll resume at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, please continue your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just before the break, Mr. Alispahic, we were -- you were telling us about the re-taking of the police station by better-armed police. How many of them were required to re-take the police station?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: By then the situation was complicated. The military, in a way, took the police station. They were physically inside the station. They had disarmed the police officers and the commander had surrendered. 20 or 30 police officers went there to re-take the station, in a manner of speaking, and reclaim it for the MUP. Their determination and their numbers simply resolved the problem because there was eventually no armed conflict when the station was re-taken. There was no casualties and no wounded. That's how the situation was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that on the same day?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And do you remember whether it was before or after the meeting you and Mr. Delic had with Caco, Celo, and units from -- people from the Delta Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think it all happened on the same day at more or less the same time. It was a critical problem being faced by the entire town, faced by all those who were in charge of tackling this problem. Delic and myself tried to do so because some people had asked us to come, and the chief of the centre, meanwhile, was solving this problem with the police. I think it more or less coincided in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which units had taken the police station?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think the units under Caco's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about some specific incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown exhibit which was MNA 204.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about a document which bears your name, signature, of the 2nd of June, 1993, which will come up on the computer screen to your left there. Now firstly, is that a document -- is that a document of which you're the author and have signed, the date of the 2nd of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May I just indicate I haven't got that on the screen - I'm sorry, Your Honours - at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe it is coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, if I'm not the only one, I'm happy, Your Honour. Your Honours, I think the Bosnian version is on the screen now, for those who have got that channel, but unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, I think it has to be released by the Prosecution. I think they have done it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we have it. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, is that a report or a communication which you wrote to the military, the Main Staff, the 2nd of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: This is one of the ways in which we communicated and one of the ways to address these institutions, the Defence Ministry, the Main Staff, and other bodies that were in charge of tackling the problem. The minister of the interior, the minister himself, the 1st Corps, and so on and so forth, this is a summary, so to speak, of the incidents caused by Ramiz Delalic. I drew up a brief report and had it delivered to these addressees. I signed the report, and this is information that we obtained through our police system. We submitted this information to other people and asked that steps be taken, that assistance be provided, to deal with these matters. The situation was difficult. There were a great many incidents. By way of an example, Delalic never agreed to have any communication with the police. He never wanted to pull over whenever he was stopped by the police. The result of these things was that he was pulled over by a police patrol once, and when the police officer searched his car they found no documents, no personal documents, and none of the car's documents. There were a number of incidents, and this is a report that speaks about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The report says: "On that occasion he insulted the police and the heads of the centre and the secretariat and threatened to blow up the police station." Which police station did he threaten to blow up?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all I'd like to say that this was his usual mode of behaviour and communication; secondly, I think he was referring to the station to which he had been taken or the police station whose members they -- whose members controlled him at this point in time; traffic police in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think we object to this being received into evidence. The witness has given an explanation for it which is, frankly, a suitable one to have it admitted into evidence, so the objection is quite a narrow one, and that is that Mr. Delalic was here last week and why wasn't it put to him? Now, it wasn't put to him at all. And in fact it has to be commented that the Defence -- the Prosecution case wasn't put to him, so it's really a question of the Prosecution putting documents to a witness who's got something to say about that document that really should be acceded to. Now, otherwise, this witness is plainly qualified to look at this and say it is his document. Plainly it should be admitted in the normal course of events. In this case I object to it not because of anything that Mr. Alispahic says but because it was never shown to Mr. Delalic last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think your objection has some point in it, and the -- but however, I believe this document was drafted by this witness and this witness testified to that effect. We have no doubt to believe that this document is relevant and has some probative value on that. As for the question why this document was not put to the previous witness, we assume that it's something within the strategy from the Prosecution, it's their way to present their case. But on the document itself as well as the testimony of this witness, we see no problem for it to be admitted into the evidence. So it's admitted into the evidence, and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- Court Deputy will assign a number to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P204, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the next document, which is Prosecution 65 ter 165, which is ERN 0403-4969.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 429.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just note that the English translation, I just noticed, appears to have missed the date of the document, which is the 28th of June, 1993. On the Bosnian version -- sorry, the Bosnian original has a date of 28/6/93 under the number 17-1/01- handwritten 29th of June at the top. So if that could just be corrected for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just have a look at that document, Mr. Alispahic, and the information in that document. Firstly, is that a Ministry of the Interior document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Can we have the whole document shown, please? This document belongs to the Ministry of the Interior, security services centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's a signature --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry. There's a name or a signature on the bottom. It starts with Munja and then it says "illegible." Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Alibabic, the former chief of the security services centre, Alibabic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, could you please speak up for the interpreters, speak a little more loudly.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The name is Munir Alibabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And was he the person who succeeded you in the job as chief of the Sarajevo police?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this person document or hearing or knowing about the information contained in it -- okay, one question at a time. I understand the objection that's coming. Starting over again, Mr. Alispahic. Are you aware of the information which is contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this particular document at the time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I can't say that I saw the document at the time, but I'm familiar with the information contained in this document, the incidents that occurred, as well as this incident at the clinical centre in Kosevo in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there an objection to the document? I mean, I can have the witness give the evidence orally or the document can be tendered if he says it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, there is an objection to the document. If it's going to assist the Court, the witness may say what he knows about it, so long as it's not too remote. That's a matter for the Court what level of hearsay you wish to hear, frankly. We don't know what level of hearsay it is now. The witness may have heard something, and it would be best to see where he got the information and then it may be that it would be admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, you can ask some questions concerning this document to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you were familiar with the information in the document. Where did you obtain your information from?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: All the information in relation to any of the incidents that occurred in the town of Sarajevo at the time was part of the collective information obtained by the Ministry of the Interior. A summary is made to indicate that such-and-such thing happened at such-and-such time in such-and-such place. You don't go into detail, you can always check this with the Ministry of the Interior. This is the terminology of our work. It was in this way that I obtained any information, and the same applies to this particular piece of information. Very often it was in direct communication with the chief of the centre, specifically Mr. Alibabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you remember about this particular incident, that's the one of the clinical hospital? It says there on the 26th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness is permitted to answer that question, it should be established where he learned this particular information, if he can remember that - it may be that he can, it may be that he can't - and if he got it from Mr. Alibabic. The next question is: Where did Mr. Alibabic get it from? It may be that there's no valid objection to this being given but it may be that there is. It would be important to establish what level, as I said earlier, of hearsay we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you read carefully the answer of this witness to the previous question, I believe that the witness testified that he learned of this information as a part of the collective information obtained by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I -- well, I agree with that, Your Honour, and that's why I raise the issue that he may know more than that. But it really depends, Your Honours. If Your Honour sees that as a sufficient basis for him to say what the information was that he learned through operative channels, well, then I don't have an objection -- I don't have a valid objection if that's your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we believe that is enough, so this document is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P429.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution 65 ter 152, 0147-4761. Now, this is a document dated, for the record, the 6th of July, 1993, headed "Certain intelligence connected to the incident between a number of soldiers from the 10th Mountain Brigade and members of the BH MUP in Stari Grad area."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 430.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: First question is: Is this a document from the minister -- Ministry of the Interior, the state security part of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The document is somewhat illegible in the sense that there's a shade right on top. But this is a document produced by the state security service, one of the segments of the interior. It's to do with the work of the secret service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Can you please scroll down?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of document is it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It says, "Information."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you -- if you've having difficulty reading it, do you want -- would a paper copy of this particular document be clearer for you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: If it's no problem. I can say that this is a document produced by the Ministry of the Interior; more specifically, state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of document is it, though? In what category does it fall?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think there should be an attachment to go with this document to indicate who the document was addressed to and at whose request it was produced, who it was for. According to the method employed by the secret service, this document would be entitled "Information." If you have a document with that status, that means it analyses certain events and certain forms of behaviour on the ground. As a matter of principle, a document like this should comprise verified information. Everything that's in it should be verified because the end user of this document must enjoy the privilege of full information. And we know who the users of these documents were at the time; the president of the -- the Prime Minister, Hadziefendic, and some other officials, I think. So this is a report which has an objective. The objective is to give a summary of security-related information in the area of Stari Grad municipality. And this again has to do with the commanders of the 9th and 10th Brigades, their behaviour, and their actions within this environment. At the time, Jozo Jozic was the chief of the SDB, state security service, and I think he signed this report. In the lower right-hand corner of the document you can see his signature and a remark that he added.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What does the remark say? Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: If we can zoom in, then perhaps I can say. I think it says here, "For Vikic, Dragan Vikic." This is about certain threats made against the commander of the special unit Vikic, then on the right-hand side you have Jozic. That's what it says -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What does, "For Vikic, Dragan Vikic" mean?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. There's a reference to it in the main body of the text. If I can have a minute to read through it. I think this particular passage next to the remark that was added is important for one reason. There was operative information available that there had been an information leak among the military bodies that some things would happen or that there would be replacements in those units. So people were advising each other on how to act in that situation. It says that some of the members should transfer to Musan Topalovic, Caco's, unit in order to feel safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, are you familiar with this type of document from your position as the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The content of the document I'm familiar with, the form of the document, the information contained therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you -- was that the sort of document you would have ordinarily seen in the course of your work as the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I had to have been informed with this document, with its contents, in view of the office I held, especially since this document speaks of the situation that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On page 3 of the English, and I don't have the Bosnian in front of me at the moment, it says: "We also have significant intelligence that on the 3rd of June Sefer Halilovic held a meeting with Ramiz Delalic and the command staff of the Delta Unit. On that occasion, they advocated an attack against the Presidency of the republic and the capture of some Presidency members." Now, a moment ago you said you were familiar with the information in the document. Are you aware of the source of the information for that particular portion of the document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the state security service, the sources of the information could be as follows: The information could come from an associate, it could come from the mass media or some other source.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there an objection to the tender of this document? I anticipate there might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honour. Once again, Your Honours have ruled against me in relation to operative-information type of documents. I won't repeat my argument there. I'll just simply say I object to it on that ground, say no more. With respect to this document, it goes a little bit further. I take it these documents are being led as operative information, simply as a matrix of information that was available to the authorities at the time, rather than as to the truth of their contents. Now, if that's the case, what I'd submit is that this particular document is of relatively limited weight, and that's a matter for Your Honours to weigh. If it's being led as to its truth, well, I object to it absolutely, of course. But the Prosecutor could say that it's being led as operative information only, in which case I have the objection that it's remote and not probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, would you please ask this witness whether this witness has seen this document before and when was that, especially in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: His answer a moment ago was: "I had to have been informed with this document, its contents, in view of the office I held at the time."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, do you remember now specifically seeing this particular document at the time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I will repeat once again. I cannot confirm that I saw this document in its current form, but it is certain that I read this document and that I'm familiar with the contents of the document. The document originated in the state security service, not as an operative document as you seem to understand it. A document can be composed on the basis of several sources and information, the majority of which must come from very reliable sources such as communication means, reliable sources of information, various associates, and so on. I think that this is the document of the state security service, that it dealt with the burning issue at the time, and that it definitely reached the end users in the then-government. Finally, I think that if you looked around, this document should also exist in the BH army, or rather in the military security services, and also with some political establishments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after hearing the explanations by this witness, we decided that this document is admitted into the evidence, while bearing in mind that certain information contained in this document is not necessarily true, especially for some allegations which are not pled in the indictment. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P430.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P207. For the record, to make the transcript easier, that's a report of the 19th of September, 1993, of the Ministry of the Interior state security service in Sarajevo, referring to an incident on the 8th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just have a look at that document, Mr. Alispahic, which is signed by Jozo --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Could you please go back to the beginning of the document, to the upper portion of the document. This is the signature of Jozo Jozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to ask you briefly: Are you familiar with the document and the contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Similar to many other documents, it is hard to say that I am familiar with this document. In view of the office that I held, I could retain certain information, verify, solve problems, and so on. I am familiar with this incident. It took place near Pazaric, Pazarici. In the morning when this incident took place, Jozo Jozic and many -- Alibabic reacted to this incident. We informed the military security service regarding this. And what actually happened was that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, attacked the policemen. A fight broke out, in the course of which I think one policeman was gravely wounded.
