I think that it almost erupted into a firearms incident. The chief of the military security service was informed about this incident which was started by Ramiz Delalic, Celo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was anyone else in the military, to your knowledge, informed about that besides Jusuf Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say -- I couldn't say whether anybody else was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown 65 ter Exhibit 150, which is 0218-2500. The document, for the purposes of the record, is dated the 15th of June, 1993, is headed "Official Note," and purports to emanate from the SBD Sarajevo, security services centre, SBD of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 431.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I indicate this is the document I raised at the start of proceedings today, and I will be taking an objection to it. But it will be necessary, I suppose, for Your Honours to rule on it, that you know what's in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think at this stage we'll allow this document to be used, then we'll see whether we should have it admitted into evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this a document from the -- emanating from the Ministry of the Interior when you were the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's headed "Official --"

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: This is the document of the security services centre, the Sarajevo SBD sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's headed "Official Note." What sort of document is this?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: This document is, in accordance with the classification that existed, the lowest-ranking document in terms of its reliability, which means that the information contained here had to be further verified. The note was composed on the basis of information received from a source, from an associate. So the information was compiled on the basis of what was received from that source, and the information needed to be further verified and confirmed from other -- needed to be confirmed on the basis of other sources or other material that had already been verified. The document describes certain incidents which took place in the Jablanica sector and involved certain members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with the contents. I read the document. I know that there was a vast number of incidents taking place down there caused by the army members who were stationed there. This is what I know based on the information that I received. I don't want to go into details regarding any single incident but will simply say that on account of these incidents, the members of these units were returned to Sarajevo. I think that it would be very difficult to say that the information contained in this document is fully reliable, because it speaks about rapes and some other grave incidents, but other information could be reliable. The official note, in accordance with the method adopted by the Ministry of the Interior, does not normally reach the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the information in that was further verified or confirmed from other sources?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that in accordance with the regular procedure, the allegations contained in the notes are normally verified. I think that there was a lot of accuracy here regarding these incidents, and I think that because of that these units were sent back to Sarajevo because they engaged in misconduct while being outside of their area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the source of your information that the members of the Delta Unit and Ramiz Delalic's Sabotage Unit were sent back to Sarajevo because of some of the things mentioned in this note?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I object to this. Now what the Prosecutor's trying to do is to make this true. He's now asking whether this has been verified. Now, Your Honours, I object to this, and again without prejudice to what the witness is saying about his perceptions. It could not be relevant to the case, Your Honours, in this document because it refers specifically to Sefer Halilovic. And don't forget what it says. It says here - this is source SS saying this - that Ramiz Delalic -- sorry, that the -- a unit burned the village to the ground and the order for the destruction of the village of Klis was issued by Sefer Halilovic. If you look over the page you'll see that there's another one, that Mr. Halilovic has been planning another one. Now, I'm not criticising the witness in this regard. This is material which he's given plain evidence now, an Official Note, would not normally have reached him. But is it the Prosecution case now for the first time in this Court that Halilovic did these things? Now, that has to be clarified. Now, if that's what they're saying, they better announce that that's what they're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now -- well, however, we'll give the full opportunity for the Prosecution to exhaust their case, which means that they could ask some questions to establish the reliability of this document. And as I have already said, that at this stage we are not in a position to make a ruling concerning the admission of this document. First of all, we find that the witness testified that the need -- that information was in need of the verification and the confirmation further. And later on he also said there are lot of inaccuracies concerning some of the information which is not quite clear to us. Secondly, the allegations in this document is a very serious one. It's directly related to Mr. Halilovic, the accused of this case, and there are murders, slaughtering of the civilians, as well as rape. So it's a very serious one. And thirdly, I wonder if these kind of allegations were really pleaded in the indictment or not. But since this document is in use now, we'll allow the Prosecution to ask some questions concerning this document. Of course, in the cross-examination the Defence has the full opportunity to ask some questions concerning with this document. And later on, I believe we'll be in a better position to make a ruling on the admission of this document. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Alispahic, was related to the source of your information that members of the Delta Unit and Ramiz Delalic and his Sabotage Unit were sent back to Sarajevo because of some of the things mentioned in this particular document. What I want to know is: What did you hear or how did you come to find out they were sent back because of that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: There are two questions posed here. One has to do with the document, and the other deals with how I found out about these things, about the incidents and the problems taking place there on the ground and the members of the army who were there in the field. At the time when this document was created, I never heard from my associates or through any other channels about the allegations contained here regarding General Halilovic. Further, the problems posed by the army members named here in the document, I learned of that through police chiefs in Jablanica and other places through regular briefing and reporting. Members of certain units -- and I have to say that this refers to individuals. The army at the time was involved in defensive operations, and these incidents were caused by individuals. I received information about incidents. They told me that these army members were down there creating trouble for Bosniak and Croatian population, that they were causing disorder down there in that entire area. From the same sources, from police sources, I learned that they had been sent back to Sarajevo. I think that the source who wrote this document which deals with the murders, burning of villages and some other grave events either augmented it or even invented some of the things mentioned here, because I cannot believe to this day that General Halilovic would have issued any such instructions to these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said, before the discussion between the Presiding Judge and Mr. Morrissey that: "I don't want to go into details regarding any single incident but will simply say that on account of these incidents members of the units were returned to Sarajevo. I think it would be very difficult to say that the information contained in this document is fully reliable because it speaks about rapes and some other grave incidents, but other information could be reliable." Based upon what you heard at the time through your own sources, which -- and you've already said that you don't believe that Mr. Halilovic ordered the things described there. Based on the information you had at the time through your own sources, what is your assessment of what is reliable or could be reliable in that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I now do object to this. To ask a witness what he thinks could be reliable about a document that he might have seen is really way to remote, and I object to it on that simple ground alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe the word "could" is not properly used, but I believe that Mr. Re is entitled to ask what is reliable in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you consider, Mr. Alispahic, based upon your sources, what you heard at the time, to be reliable in that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I'm qualifying that question to be as fair as I possibly can to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that based on the entire document except for matters relating to General Halilovic and him ordering -- I think that it says in there ordering for villages to be burned down and people to be killed and so on, other than that, everything else is pretty accurate. What is accurate is these army members engaged in vandalism, in mistreatment, that they got drunk, that they caused damage, that they also damaged their own reputation and that of the BH army. I can't tell you anything further than that because at the time I did not have the information at my disposal, but I can tell you now that I don't believe that what is stated about the general in the document is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And just for the record, the sake of the record, the document is referring to incidents in the territory of Jablanica and Konjic in May 1993, particularly in the village of -- Croatian village of Klis, K-l-i-s. It's on our list. I note the Defence objection. I won't move to tender it at the moment, because I understand there will be an argument about it, and I'll move on, if that's acceptable to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about an incident in October 1993 involving shelling of the Ministry of the Interior building. What happened?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: This incident is perhaps one in a series of certain types of incidents. Some incidents were verbal, some incidents could be qualified as provocations, and some incidents involved the threat of firearms use. Caco's people had an aversion -- a high level of aversion towards the Ministry of the Interior and its members. Perhaps they even felt somewhat unsafe in view of all of the things they had committed. And as a result, they themselves caused these incidents. One of such incidents involved two grenades of a small calibre fired from the city itself. This was all established on the basis of the on-site investigation. Based on our information, such grenades at the time were -- existed only in Caco's unit. This is one of the recorded incidents. I mean the information regarding it is recorded in our service and was investigated and the factual situation was established. This information was further investigated by the security service. This is all I can say about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to clarify what you said, I asked you about an incident involving shelling of the MUP building in October 1993, and you said that there were two small-calibre -- two grenades of a small calibre fired from the city. Are you saying there that two grenades were fired at the ministry building from within Caco's area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, before the witness answers that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- could I just point out that this incident is in October of 1993 and it couldn't be relevant to Mr. Halilovic's guilt. I don't understand it's being put that he fired those missiles, Your Honours, and in my submission it's just irrelevant to the charges before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage I'm not quite sure when Mr. Halilovic was released from the post because of the Trebevic operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think the evidence is already admitted that he was arrested on the 26th of -- or the 27th of October, and I believe it to be the 1st of November. And I think there's an order already in evidence about that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I -- at this moment, I fail to see the point from the Prosecution. Maybe if we allow the Prosecution to ask a few more questions, the picture will be more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may be so. I am obliged to take the objections when they arise. I'm certainly not doing so to be difficult. I just have to take them now. I can't play a violin later on, I must take them now, so I do take the objection now. I hear Your Honour's ruling about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let us see how far the Prosecution could go. If they are really irrelevant to our case, I think this kind of evidence should be barred. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, I was asking you just to clarify what happened, just to summarise what happened. Are you saying that from within the area of the 10th --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the -- let me stop there. I think he said from the city, from my recollection, Your Honours. Perhaps I've missed something in the evidence, but I don't think I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's from the city. But the witness also testified that that kind of special hand grenade was only available in the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just seeking some clarity from what you were saying to -- are you saying -- perhaps I could ask it this way: Are you saying that two special grenades, of only a type that Caco had, were fired at the Ministry of the Interior building?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I'll define it like this: We at the Ministry of the Interior viewed this as two shells that were fired from positions occupied by members of the 10th Mountain Brigade, Caco's brigade. This was preceded by certain actions, an on-site investigation obtaining operative information, and then based on all of these findings and investigations, the MUP took the position that I've described. That was the position of the Ministry of the Interior then and it still is. As I said, those grenades were no special grenades. We had very few anyway. These were rather low-calibre grenades which were seen to be for what they were. They caused a minor amount of damage. And with the benefit of hindsight and knowing what weapons were around, those low-calibre shells could not have arrived from more distant positions. It was ascertained that the shells had arrived from that direction, both on the operative level and by an on-site investigation. We at the Ministry of the Interior have a special department for counter-sabotage protection. Those were qualified people doing their job, and that's all I'm saying, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was that incident?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: That incident occurred at the same time as everything else we're talking about, these recurring incidents between the police on the one hand and some members of the army on the other, but I can't give you a specific date. It was prior to the Trebevic operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to say approximately how long before Trebevic, which was in late October 1993, that this happened?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Not long before. Roughly about the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to move now to the area of Operation Neretva and the operation in Herzegovina in 1993. You've already given evidence earlier that special police units were used in combat fairly regularly by the army. Did you attend a meeting in Zenica involving military -- high military officials?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I gave a statement in 2001 and I said something about this question that you're asking me. I think it was back in 2001, roughly the same time of the year as now. I think it was an expanded meeting of the military leadership that took place in Zenica. The meeting was about the situation as it then prevailed throughout the army and on the ground and in relation to combat operations. All the senior officers who were able to attend were there. As far as I remember, among those unable to attend was the senior officer from the Bihac Corps. Bihac was surrounded at the time and I don't think he was able to make it. There was Rasim Delic, there was General Sefer Halilovic, Hadzihasanovic, and other officers in command -- corps commanders. I was also there in my capacity as the interior minister. I had been invited to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why were you invited to attend?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I'll give you my opinion as to why I was invited and why I attended. I think after Delic became the number one man in the army, he wanted to have this meeting. He wanted to ensure that there would be progress, in a manner of speaking, in the army, regardless whether it was concerning combat operations or the other segments. There were a lot of problems in Sarajevo; the incidents that we've spoken about and the difficult situation that prevailed. The situation at the front line was no less difficult. We had a situation where there was intense fighting going on with the HVO on the one side and the Serb aggressor army on the other. The situation was critical, and I think I was invited to that meeting because I was the interior minister at the time and because the Ministry of the Interior by resubordinating their own special units, which may to some extent have been merely a symbolic act, paid a great contribution to defending Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that was the reason, or rather those were the reasons I was invited to attend and help on behalf of the Ministry of the Interior in whichever way I could, give assistance to the overall effort made by the BH army in defending Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, do you remember the date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but it was mid-August 1993, perhaps second half of August, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many days did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I remember I was there for the first day when most of the matters were raised, most of the problems brought up by those attending. Senior officers, Supreme Command staff, corps commanders, they spoke about certain problems. There was a debate following their contributions. It was clear that the priority was combat, to liberate all the territories where it was possible to do something. I was there on the first day, and I know from my conversations later with General Delic and other officers, because we were frequently in touch and we frequently socialised, that the meeting went on to define everything that was said on the first day. But there was no longer any need for me to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to show you the front page of one document, P1 -- Exhibit P109. And while that's being found I'll ask you about things that were discussed at the meeting. Mr. Halilovic -- did you say Mr. Halilovic was present?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was. All of the army's commanders were there, the whole Supreme Command staff; the inner sanctum plus the corps commanders, with the exception of the Bihac commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Your Honour motioning for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think we have to take a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, we are at Zenica meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have a document in front of you which is P109 just to your left there? I just want you to comment -- it's got a date of the 21st and 22nd of August, 1993, in Zenica a meeting was held with the topic "Most Prominent Achievements." It goes down a bit and says, "The first day of the meeting, Minister of the Interior Bakir Alispahic was also present." Is that document referring to the particular meeting you attended in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think it must be that meeting. I've never seen this document, but the names given in this document indicate that it must be the same meeting. I couldn't comment on this document as such, but I can say what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Its substance or anything related to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's why I'm only showing you the first page, only the dates and the participants, that's all I'm interested in in relation to that particular document.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, I just want to move to things that were discussed at that particular meeting. You said that Mr. Halilovic was there. Were any forthcoming military operations discussed when you were there on the first day?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. There was a lot of discussion, but the focus was on military operations, what to do, which operations to carry out, which were realistic and which were not in terms of what the BH army could manage. General Halilovic and everyone else discussed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any forthcoming military operations involving special MUP units discussed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It was said that an operation should be prepared. Prepared. What does that mean? To carry out the necessary steps within the army, to draw up a plan for an operation near Mostar, because that was the area that was in jeopardy at the time and the jeopardy could have become even greater and the situation more complex. The road between Jablanica and Mostar had been cut and it was necessary to take steps. The assessment given at this meeting was that it was necessary to carry out military activities in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was the involvement, if any, of special MUP units to be?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It was for the purposes of this operation that I was requested to send the Laste special unit as well as sufficient equipment in order to relieve the army of those duties. The idea was to supply them with some amount of equipment for the first actions. In military terms it's called a combat set, for the unit to be given equipment, a combat kit, and for this unit to be resubordinated to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the framework of this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who made that request of you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think it was also made by General Halilovic as well as by General Delic, which I considered to be perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you consider it to be normal?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I considered it to be normal because I based myself on my experience of cooperation between the army and the police. Previously, the police was involved to the extent that it could in terms of the police officers that were available or equipment. The police always joined combat activity whenever possible. And this operation that was to be carried out implied that my ministry should give whatever assistance it could, and this is how it was presented, as a serious plan. The area was in jeopardy, and it was for these reasons that I considered their request to be a perfectly reasonable one. I agreed and complied with their request.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the operation given a name or did it go by a name at that particular point, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember right now. The day when I was in Zenica, there was some speculation regarding the name of that operation. In military terminology, all these operations and actions, to the extent that I understood, were given a name. And then this name is used to cover a whole range of activities. But I can't be certain that I obtained that kind of information in Zenica at the time. The only thing that did happen is I agreed that I would resubordinate my special unit to the army for the purposes of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you later learn of the name of that particular operation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Later, based on my contacts and conversations with different people, with different police officers, based on what I learned from the media, I learned that the name was Operation Neretva. I never considered whether this was an official name that was designated because it was in the Neretva River valley or just down the river from there. I considered the name to be a logical choice and came to the conclusion that it was the official name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From what was said at the meeting and the request of you for your Laste Unit, what was your understanding of who was to command that particular operation towards Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honours. That's a compound sort of a question. It should be made clear whether or not this witness is saying that a commander was appointed or foreshadowed at the meeting, not mixed between that and something that was later heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question was directly directed towards what was said at that meeting and it's confined only to that meeting, Your Honour, at the moment. It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that there's two questions in your question. So you may ask one, then another.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was to command the operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I knew, General Sefer Halilovic commanded the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think I learned this and understood this at the meeting itself, based on what people were saying, based on what we were talking about as to what was to be done. It was known that the special police unit was a good, well-trained unit, and he asked personally for this unit to be re-assigned to him for the purposes of this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that unit actually assigned to that operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Stop there for a moment, please. Your Honours, that question in military terms is not capable of being meaningful. Units aren't assigned to an operation; they're assigned under the command of a person. And for the purposes of Mr. Halilovic's charges, it should be asked -- that should be related to him; was it actually assigned to him or to some other person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe the word is not a proper word. Maybe Mr. Re could change for another word to convey your idea. I'm not a military man. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, you used the word "re-assigned." Did you mean - at the risk of leading - resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In military terminology, yes, if I accepted that a police unit would be given to the army to use, then this unit would be under the command of the army and not under the command of the police, if that's the explanation you're seeking. It was to be resubordinated, and it was military bodies that would then be in command of these -- this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: My apologies. This is how it works in practice, and there were situations like this, both before and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm actually interested in is what happened. You used the word "assigned," that I understood you to mean was sent to the military. How were they sent to the military? What was the process? Was an order given? Did you give an order? What happened?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Certainly based on our agreement, an obligation was defined and then the ministry issued an order, a document that must still be somewhere in the ministry, to send this unit to the area of combat operations and resubordinated the unit to the BH army. There's a document that indicates a list of police members and specifies the number of police members that would be reporting to a predetermined location, and that's what our agreement implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from your involvement in the meeting at Zenica, did you have any further involvement in the planning or the preparations of that particular operation, that is Operation Neretva?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: No, I was in no way involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about in relation to the participation of the police units? Did you ever have any discussions with any of the people at the Zenica meeting after the meeting about their participation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think there was any need. The relationship between the army and the police was a well-known one. Everything was defined. A unit would have its commander. The commander would have his deputy commander. All the weapons would be there and all the equipment. This unit would then be sent to an area and report to one of the local commanders, who would then use the unit as they saw fit and according to their own plan that was being implemented. There was no need for me to intervene, because that would have meant interference with the matters of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the Laste Unit actually sent to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you in the Herzegovina area when the Laste Unit arrived there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In the context of my own plan -- first of all, let me explain that the Laste Special Unit, in terms of its establishment, was part of the security services centre in Sarajevo; my position at the time was the minister of the interior. Within the framework of my duties, my plans, I visited Herzegovina, knowing, among other things, that the unit would be used, that an operation would take place, and that combat activities would be carried out. It was my intention, if necessary, to seek assistance from other police bodies, should they be approached for help by be it the special unit, be it the army, so that they would help whenever it was necessary. Another thing I planned was to visit the Konjic police station, the Jablanica police station, the Mostar security services centre, and this was my first visit upon becoming minister. It was the first time that any of the government officials visited Mostar because Mostar was physically isolated. I'm not talking about official representatives of the government; I'm talking about army members. That's what I did in Herzegovina, and these were my whereabouts in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did the Laste Unit get to Herzegovina and where did it go to upon arrival?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The Laste Unit was sent on behalf of the security services centre in Sarajevo. Once this was approved at the ministerial level and once this was endorsed by me following our agreement with the army leaders, the Laste Unit received a written order to go to Herzegovina. This written order detailed who the unit commander would be, who the deputy commander would be, where they should go, and who they should report to. So the Laste Unit being in Herzegovina on the one hand and the minister being there on the other, these are two unrelated matters. The Laste Unit was involved in a military activity, and the minister was going about his own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did they get there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: First of all, as far as I know, the Laste Unit was made up out of two formations of that unit. One formation had left the besieged Sarajevo, and the other one was already in Tarcin. This is where these two formations linked up. The unit was united, so to speak, and was sent, deployed, to Konjic, albeit its final destination was Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the strength of the two units combined?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Actually, this is one single unit, it is just composed of two segments, and there were about 50 police members in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said they linked up in Tarcin and it was deployed to Konjic and the final destination was Mostar. Did the unit go to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I must emphasise here that the time of my departure and the time of the departure of the unit did not coincide, meaning that they needed more time to depart as a unit and to unite. I linked up with the unit in Jablanica, intending to arrive in Mostar together with them. I can't remember the names of the villages, but it was in the vicinity of the mountains near Jablanica that we were at the time. We walked. We had no means of transportation, and our trip took about 16 hours before we arrived in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying you accompanied the unit from the mountains near Jablanica to Mostar on foot?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. We walked together on foot. It so happened that I walked with them the entire time. The trip was an arduous one. It was very difficult. We had to travel during nighttime. We couldn't travel during daytime due to the enemy activities. So we started during the night. Some part of the trip we covered during the day, but the critical one took place at night. The unit went to the location where they were supposed to report to, to rest from the trip in order to prepare for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was in the -- in command of that unit when you were accompanying them on foot from Jablanica to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that the commander's name was Zeljko, and the deputy's last name was Tufo. It was quite a long time ago, but these two people were the commanders of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you wearing a uniform or in civilian clothes when you accompanied this unit, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that I was in uniform then. Most of the officials from the civilian organs at the time wore uniforms for practical reasons. Police members do know -- do wear uniforms very frequently, and I myself spent quite a lot of time in a uniform during the war. It was practically impossible to go to Mostar wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that a police uniform or a military uniform, or was there a difference?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that at the time they did not differ at all. The insignia was different. It was very difficult to obtain uniforms, so the uniforms were the same. I don't know, how should I qualify this uniform? This was a type of a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said the unit went to the location where they were supposed to report to prepare for combat. Where was that and who did they report to?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think that they went to the command of the corps in Mostar. I think that it was the 4th Corps at the time. Arif Pasalic was the commander, the corps commander. I know that I met him on that occasion. We had meetings and discussed the current issues. So the unit reported to the corps command. I also had a meeting with the chief of the security services centre in Mostar; his name was Ramo Maslesa. We discussed police problems and other issues from the police domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From when was the Laste Unit subordinated to the military? Was it from when you got to Mostar or from some other point?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid any confusion, let me just reiterate that I am not a military expert. However, I believe that when the order was issued for the unit to be deployed and to report to a certain command, that that in itself was an act of resubordination, which meant that from that moment on that unit was a part of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the Laste Unit go into combat as part of Operation Neretva after having arrived in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a very difficult situation in Mostar at the time as well in the military sense. Based on the information I received from Ramo Maslesa and from the security services centre, the Laste Unit was given very difficult positions somewhere in the vicinity of Santiceva Street. And these positions were difficult because they were frequently subjected to heavy fire, and the unit was thus assigned a very difficult task. In the very beginning, some members were gravely wounded and I think that one member of the unit was even killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I think I stayed there very briefly. Based on my recollection, I can tell you what activities I had there to give you an idea of the -- of how much time I spent there. We had to go back during nighttime, therefore I think that I spent just one day in Mostar. That means that we arrived in the morning hours. During the day we had meetings. We rested to the extent possible. And as it was summertime and the days are longer, we had to wait in order to leave after the nightfall, to cover the area that was dangerous. I must say that both when entering and leaving Mostar, we were exposed to the enemy fire of the HVO. The vehicle that I was travelling in was hit by the HVO fire. We had to stop and we had a small crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who were you with?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Since I was travelling together with the unit, I only had my escorts with me. I had a driver and one security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you said you were in a vehicle. You left Mostar in a vehicle. Where were you travelling to?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we were unable to travel any large distances by car. That means that apart from 10 to 15 kilometres that we travelled in vehicles, everything else we had to walk. We walked through the mountains. And from Mostar to Jablanica, we travelled in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do when you got back to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In principle, the minister of the interior normally visits police stations. This is the first place that they report to to see what the situation is like in the police. This is where they are briefed, this is where they receive certain information, this is where they get acquainted with the work conducted by the police. Every police station normally receives a dispatch announcing that a minister would arrive for a visit. This is something regulated by the ministry regulations. That means that there is some type of a control of movement of the highest officials. Police stations are always informed about this in order to provide security or any assistance the officials may need.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you visit the police station in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the police station, both in Jablanica and Konjic. So when I'm discussing these matters, I mean to say that I visited all police stations. At the time, I visited the Jablanica police station and met with part of its commanding staff. The commander of the police station then was Zebic. Since Jablanica -- Jablanica and Konjic are quite near, sometimes the police chief from Jablanica would come to Konjic or vice versa, because these two places are very near each other and both of them have police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's the distance between the two places?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Since this is not far, one could cover the distance in a car. I think it's only 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Konjic police station then?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I remember only the chief of the police station, who was Jasmin Guska. And in Jablanica it was Zebic, Emin Zebic. So the chief of the police station is the number one person and the commander of the station is someone who is below him. I think the name is Emin Zebic, E-m-i-n, who was the chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Zebic -- Mr. Emin Zebic, did you see him when you came to a police station after your return from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where and when was that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: At the police station in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the meeting about?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: When I arrived there, I think that Zebic was there and perhaps a few more people. Emin Zebic and perhaps a couple of his associates were there. Zebic told me then that they had certain problems, major problems, and he wanted to hear my opinion as to what should be done. Then further into the conversation, he said that there had been operative information to the effect that the army members from Sarajevo - that's what he said - or perhaps members from Celo's and Caco's unit, had killed some civilians, committed a massacre in a village, and this was the information I received initially. Later on, Zebic explained, once we started discussing the problem, that he had sent his policemen to the area to establish what had happened, to identify the problem; however, his policemen encountered the police patrol who banned them from entering the area, saying that the area was under their control and that these policemen could not conduct any kind of an investigation there. That was the attitude of the people manning the checkpoint in the area where all the events had happened. Since he knew about certain incidents, he knew about this also based on our communications, he knew that members of these units were involved in these incidents, therefore he did not dare enter into a conflict with them and insist upon entering the area because there would have definitely been an armed conflict. Zebic knew, just as I knew, that in the area of combat operations where army is conducting combat operations, police has no access and that these tasks are normally carried out by the military police. Therefore, Zebic, at his own initiative and also pursuant to my instructions, tried to gather some information, tried to establish whether the information that they had was true. I supported him in his efforts and I tasked him with collecting as much information as possible and uncovering as much as possible, and then informing the Ministry of the Interior about that so that upon my arrival in Sarajevo I would have as much information as possible about the security information. That's all I can tell you regarding this incident. In addition to that, we also went into some other problems. Zebic complained that he had certain problems because there was a large number of refugees in Jablanica. The refugees were from the Stolac area and from Herzegovina. They had many problems in finding accommodation for the refugees, providing food for them. I think that the security situation deteriorated there. He complained about these problems. I think that we tried at the time to ask the civilian authorities in Jablanica municipality to assist us in finding solutions in order to avoid further complications.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to clarify one thing before we stop, and that's a moment ago you said Zebic told you his police had encountered the police patrol who banned them from entering the area. Did you -- it may be the transcript, but did you actually say a police patrol or something else?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the policemen were prevented from reaching the area where the incident had taken place. They were prevented by the military patrol, or rather, the patrol of the military police. I can't be more specific than that now. I can't tell you whether these were just ordinary soldiers or members of the military police. They were soldiers, members of the unit stationed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, we have to stop now for today. And as I did to other witnesses, I have to remind you that during your stay in The Hague you are still under the oath, so do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Madam Usher will show you out of the room. I will see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the Defence has something to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could we just move briefly to the private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. As briefly as I possibly can respond, and talking as slowly as I can for the interpreters, the Prosecution rejects almost everything that is in the motion that was filed today. The first thing they object -- the Defence objects to is the expertise. We've already made our position as clear as we possibly can, that the general is as qualified, we say, as any other general who can give evidence on this -- an opinion on this important point. From my own experience here in cases I've been in, in the Strugar case there were three military experts called. One is a shelling expert, that was Colonel Poje. General Zorc gave evidence from the Slovenian army, General Pringle gave evidence for the Prosecution from the British army. In the Hadzihasanovic case, General Reinhardt, from the German army, gave evidence; and of course General Karavelic gave evidence for the Defence in that case. These are all people who are giving opinions in 7(3) cases on command and control responsibilities and the duties and what a commander can reasonably be expected to do in circumstances. That's where we lead it -- that's the basis upon which we seek to lead the very brief report of -- or expert opinion of General Ridgway. They also attack his qualifications. I know -- his CV doesn't quite point it out, but he has a master of philosophy in international relations in -- from Cambridge. He told us on Friday that he -- part of that was international law. So, I mean, that's an extra qualification. His CV only refers to Cambridge but that's what I'm told he actually did at Cambridge. His length of experience and his position there now must qualify him as someone who is entitled to give an opinion on -- an opinion -- and it's only an opinion on command and control. Again they say it invades and usurps the role of the Chamber. We just don't see it. He's not saying whether Mr. Halilovic is innocent or guilty or fulfilled his duties, all he would be saying is: This is what a commander should do, would be expected, would be reasonable in certain circumstances. That's all. It's up to the Trial Chamber to apportion weight or to believe him or to disbelieve him. And the report of Mr. Ridgway could well certainly assist the Defence -- sorry, I withdraw that. The only -- the only complaint, in our submission, which could have any legs is that of timing. All the other matters we've discussed -- we've answered, and the continued complaint about which part of international law we're relying on, I think Your Honour Judge Liu dealt with that at the Status Conference. I can't say anything else about international humanitarian law, we all know where we're going with that, but the only complaint we say which could be justified would be timing. But our response to that is they have the report, they must know, they must have their own view based upon their own experts, Brigadier Dzambasovic, Mr. Mettraux who's written a book in the area, and their own expertise in the Bosnian army, consultancies over the last few years as to what they say Mr. Halilovic's duties were, assuming you're in command. They can't be taken by surprise by anything that General Ridgway is saying at this point. There's nothing new, there's nothing novel, it's just to fill a gap in the Prosecution case to provide the Trial Chamber with an opinion which we say will assist. And we say that they've had the report since last Friday. There must be sufficient time to cross-examine now. If there isn't, well, let's deal with it when it comes to it, when he gives his evidence. And the general has said he may be available on the weekend. He said anything's possible. It may be possible to schedule a weekend session if it comes to that. So in our submission, it's there, we're ready to go with it, the Defence should be ready to meet it, and we'll assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your timely reply to the motions filed by the Defence. I think at this stage this Bench is not in the position to make the rulings on the spot. We'll consider the submissions by both parties, and I hope tomorrow after we hear the witness we'll be in a better position to do so. Well, we're about seven minutes past 7.00, so I apologise to the interpreters and to all the people working for this trial. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
